title: Accidents happen — ter- and ke-…-an
goal: Talk about the things that happen to you rather than the things you do: the accidental *ter-* (*tertinggal, terjatuh, tertidur*) and the unlucky *ke-…-an* (*kehujanan, ketinggalan, kecopetan, kesiangan*). Indonesian has a grammar for bad luck, and it is very useful.
bekal: say that something happened by accident, with nobody to blame: *HP-ku tertinggal di bus*
say that something unpleasant happened to you: *aku kehujanan*, *saya kesiangan*
tell apart *dibuka* (someone opened it), *terbuka* (it is open) and *kebuka* (it came open)

notes: **Kehujanan — "rained on".** Wrap *ke-…-an* around a noun or verb and you get something that happened **to** you, usually unpleasant and never on purpose: *hujan* (rain) → *kehujanan* (caught in the rain). Sarah is not describing the weather; she is describing her bad luck. *Hari ini hujan* is a forecast, *aku kehujanan* is a complaint.

**Ketinggalan and tertinggal** both mean "left behind by accident". *Ketinggalan* is the everyday spoken one and leans towards the person who suffered: *Payungku ketinggalan* (my umbrella got left behind, poor me). *Tertinggal* is more neutral and the one you write: *Barang Anda tertinggal?* (Did you leave something behind?) on a bus notice.

**Lho, kok, walah.** *Lho* is surprise ("hey!"), *kok* is "how come?" and carries a touch of "that's odd". *Walah* is a Javanese "oh dear", which you will hear constantly in Yogya and never in a Jakarta boardroom.

**Basah kuyup, hujan deras.** Some adjectives come with a fixed partner: *basah kuyup* (soaked through), *gelap gulita* (pitch-dark), *sepi senyap* (dead quiet). *Kuyup* never appears without *basah*. And heavy rain is *hujan deras* ⚠️ not *hujan berat*, which is English wearing a batik shirt.

**Jangan-jangan — "I bet…, I'm afraid that…".** It introduces a worrying suspicion: *Jangan-jangan dia lupa* (I've a nasty feeling he forgot). It has nothing to do with the *jangan* of "don't", except that you would rather it weren't true.

**Masih untung** — "still lucky". This is a very Javanese reflex: whatever happens, find the bit that could have been worse. *Untung cuma HP, bukan dompet* (lucky it was only the phone, not the wallet). 💬 After someone's mishap, *Untung nggak apa-apa* (lucky you're OK) is the kind thing to say.

grammars.title: Ter- : it happened, nobody meant it
body: Put *ter-* on a verb root and the action becomes accidental, sudden or simply a state — there is no doer, and nobody is to blame. Compare *Pintunya dibuka* (somebody opened the door) with *Pintunya terbuka* (the door is open, or came open).
after: *Ter-* has other jobs you have already met: the superlative (*terbesar*, biggest) and fixed states (*terletak*, located; *tertulis*, written). The situation always tells you which one you are looking at.
💬 In speech many people use *ke-* for the accidental meaning: *kebuka* (came open), *kebawa* (taken by mistake), *ketiduran* (dozed off). These are casual; write *terbuka, terbawa, tertidur*.

grammars.title: Ke-…-an : it happened to me
body: *Ke-…-an* puts the **victim** first. The subject is the person who suffered, and the root is the thing that got them — rain, a thief, the late morning.

head: Word
Root
English
rows: left behind; missed (a bus, the news)
overslept, too late in the day

after: *Aku ketinggalan bus* means "I missed the bus" — the bus left me behind. *Aku ketinggalan berita* means "I missed the news" or "I'm out of the loop".

⚠️ Not every *ke-…-an* word is about bad luck. *Kebersihan* (cleanliness) and *kesehatan* (health) from Unit 9 are nouns, and in B1 you will meet *kemahalan* (too expensive). The adversative ones are nearly always about things that happen to people: weather, thieves, time, water.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Kesiangan
dialogs.intro: Two days later. Sarah arrives at half past ten; the meeting with a partner school started at nine. Mbak Nur, the office manager, is at her desk.

notes: **Kesiangan — "overslept".** Literally "caught by the late morning": *siang* is the stretch from about eleven to three, and *kesiangan* means the day got ahead of you. It is the standard word for oversleeping and for doing anything too late in the day: *Kita kesiangan, pasarnya sudah sepi* (we're too late, the market's quiet already).

**Listen to Sarah change gear.** With Mas Bayu she says *aku, nggak, makasih*; with Mbak Nur, who is her manager and precise by nature, she says *saya, tidak, mohon maaf, apakah*. Nobody told her to — the situation did. Getting this switch right matters more in an Indonesian office than getting every prefix right.

**Listrik padam** is the formal way to say the power went off; it is what the state electricity company writes in its notices. 💬 Everyone actually says *mati lampu* ("lamp died") or *listriknya mati*, even in the daytime when no lamp is on.
**Oh, pantas — "that explains it".** *Pantas* means "fitting, no wonder". 💬 The spoken form is *pantesan*: *Pantesan dia diam, lagi sakit gigi* (no wonder he's quiet, he's got toothache).

**Jam weker** is an alarm clock, from Dutch *wekker* ("waker"). Indonesian kept hundreds of Dutch household words: *handuk* (towel), *kulkas* (fridge), *kantor* (office), *setrika* (iron). *Alarm* is the alarm on your phone.

**Jangan sampai — "make sure you don't".** Stronger than plain *jangan*: it warns against a result, not an action. *Jangan sampai ketinggalan pesawat* (whatever you do, don't miss the plane). **Siap** ("ready!") is the office "will do", borrowed with a wink from the army.

grammars.title: Di-, ter- or ke-…-an?
body: The same root can be done on purpose, happen by itself, or happen to someone. Choosing the prefix is choosing who, if anyone, is responsible.

head: Form
Example
What it tells you
rows: it is open, or came open
he missed the bus (his bad luck)

after: Notice *sengaja* (on purpose) and its opposite *tidak sengaja* (by accident). *Maaf, tidak sengaja* — "sorry, I didn't mean to" — is the sentence you say after treading on someone's foot.

sections.title: More bad luck: the ke-…-an family

blocks.text: The adversative *ke-…-an* is a closed but busy family. These are the members you will need for weather, travel and city life. Each one is a whole sentence with a subject in front: *Kami kehabisan tiket.*

blocks.title: Ter- words you will read everywhere (no accident involved)
items: *terletak* — located: *Kantor kami terletak di Jalan Parangtritis.*
*terdiri dari* — consists of: *Tim kami terdiri dari lima orang.*

sections.title: When something goes wrong: what to say

blocks.text: Mishaps come with a small script. The person it happened to reports it with *ter-* or *ke-…-an*; the listener reacts with *aduh* or *waduh*, asks *kok bisa?*, and then — this is the Indonesian part — points out the luck.

blocks.text: To report a lost item at a counter, keep it simple and formal: *Permisi, Pak, HP saya tertinggal di bus nomor 4 tadi pagi.* Staff will ask *Warnanya apa?* and *Kira-kira jam berapa?* — have the colour and time ready.
